newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Delay failing climate change targets-lobby group.
newsitem.headline: Delay failing climate change targets-lobby group.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent

Governmental efforts to reduce the noxious gas emissions believed to cause global warming are failing and should be delayed to permit more realistic goals to be set, an energy industry lobby group said Wednesday.

Environmentalists were outraged at the suggestion by the London-based World Energy Council, which underlines their suspicions that energy companies and some governments have never taken the threat of global warming seriously.
WEC deputy secretary-genera Michael Jefferson said industrialised nations were way behind the targets of a return to 1990 levels of greenhouse gas emissions by 2000.
The WEC described itself as a non-government, non-commercial organisation seeking balance in energy issues.
The U.N.'s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has been seeking to force down emissions of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2).

The fight against greenhouse gases gained momentum at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, where developed countries agreed to cut CO2 output to 1990 levels by 2000. CO2 is thought to trap the sun's heat, raising the earth's temperature.
Environmentalists say the increased temperature would cause havoc with the climate. Melting polar ice would raise sea levels. Traditional agriculture would be decimated by high temperatures.
But the science of global warming has not been universally accepted. Some scientists say this is merely part of the natural cycle of warming and cooling seen through the centuries.
Others, notably IPCC scientists, say that human influence now is clear. Governments must unite to stop it.
Jefferson says the attempt has failed so far.

"We can state with some confidence that the industrialised countries' CO2 emissions are currently over five percent above 1990 levels, and in aggregate are likely to be over eight percent up on 1990 levels in the year 2000," Jefferson said in a statement after a conference entitled "The Impact of Climate Change on Business and Industry".
He said attempts in the 1990s have been ineffectual.

"It might be more realistic, if it were not interpreted as signalling further postponement of action, if industrialised countries were to move the base year from 1990 to 2000, in recognition of the failures of the 1990s," Jefferson said.

"Then legally binding targets for a realistic year, say 2020, with tougher requirements for countries which greatly overshot their 1990 emissions levels in the year 2000, with interim penalties for laggards, might be both more realistic and and more acceptable," he added.

Jefferson's remarks come as the IPCC prepares for a showdown meeting in Kyoto, Japan, in December. Environmentalists hope a protocol will be signed in Japan to build on Rio, and so-called Berlin mandate in 1995, which sought to produce targets for emissions beyhond 2000.

Nick Dunlop, director of Earth Action Network, said any fudging of agreements spells disaster. "Either governments respond with the scale of cuts that scientists say are needed, or we are facing an unprecedented global catastrophe," Dunlop said.
